warmup.q: The payments program sends each payment to the bank over a fresh connection, and closes the connection as soon as the bank answers. After a busy hour, a Linux command that lists the computer's connections shows 9,000 of them in a state called TIME-WAIT, all to the bank. The program closed every one of them. What are they?
options: Connections the bank never closed on its side, so they're stuck open and leaking
Connections the program closed first, which its computer keeps for about a minute after each close, on purpose
Goodbye messages that got lost on the way, waiting to be sent again
Payments waiting in line for a free connection to the bank
warmup.why: The side that closes a connection first keeps a small record of it after the close, and Linux keeps that record for 60 seconds. That's TIME-WAIT, and the last section explains why it exists. 9,000 of them means about 150 new connections a second (9,000 spread over 60 seconds). Each record is tiny, but each one holds a port number toward the bank, and ports are what the opening's program ran out of. The first option is the tempting one. It describes a real problem with a different name, CLOSE-WAIT, which the third section meets. The cure here is to keep a few connections open and reuse them.

sections.h: How a connection opens: three messages and two random numbers
sections.html:
Let's start small. A card reader's program sends one line over TCP, AUTH 4242 100.00, a made-up request to approve 100.00 on the card ending 4242, and a test server sends it back. We'll record every packet that passes and read them in order.

Data crosses a network in packets, small parcels of bytes with addresses on them. A computer on a network has an IP address, such as 10.10.1.10. Each program on it that talks over the network uses a port, a number from 0 to 65535 that says which program a packet is for. The kernel, the core of the operating system, handles the packets for every program on the machine. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the set of rules two kernels follow so that a stream of bytes arrives complete and in order. One TCP packet is called a segment.

In UDP and the sockets API, we got reliability by numbering each message, answering each one with an acknowledgment (an ACK) and resending after a timeout. Our numbers started at 0. TCP does the same work with two changes. It numbers every byte, not every message. And its ACK carries a number that means "I have every byte before this one". So before the first byte travels, both sides must agree where the numbering starts.

Why not always start at 0? Picture the card reader opening a connection from its port 50744 to the server's port 9000, sending a payment and closing. A second later it opens a new connection between the same two ports. Meanwhile, a segment from the first connection, stuck for a while in a router (a machine that passes packets between networks), turns up. If both connections counted from 0, the server would take those old bytes as part of the new conversation, and one payment could count twice.

So each side picks its own starting number, the initial sequence number (ISN). RFC 9293 is the document that defines TCP today. It builds the ISN from a clock that ticks every 4 microseconds, plus a scrambled number worked out from the addresses, the ports and a secret. Every connection gets a different one, and an outsider can't guess it. That matters: whoever can guess the numbers can slip their own bytes into somebody else's connection.

Each side must tell the other its number, and know that it arrived. A phone call on a bad line has the same problem. "Can you hear me?" "Yes, I hear you. Can you hear me?" "Yes." Each person needs to know their own voice gets through, so each asks and each answers. That's four messages, but the middle two fit in one, which makes three. TCP does the same. Each message is named after its flag, a marker at the front of the segment that says what kind of message it is:

  1. SYN (synchronize): the client says "my bytes start after 244700535".
  2. SYN-ACK: the server says "the next byte I expect from you is 244700536, and my bytes start after 4042781690".
  3. ACK: the client says "the next byte I expect from you is 4042781691".

This exchange is the three-way handshake. The numbers it agrees, kept in both kernels, are what we call a connection. Here are the three segments from the Try it below. They're printed by tcpdump, a program that shows every packet a network card sends or receives (-S asks for the full numbers):

10.10.1.10.50744 > 10.10.1.20.9000: Flags [S], seq 244700535, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 3966452277 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
10.10.1.20.9000 > 10.10.1.10.50744: Flags [S.], seq 4042781690, ack 244700536, win 65160, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 668285845 ecr 3966452277,nop,wscale 7], length 0
10.10.1.10.50744 > 10.10.1.20.9000: Flags [.], ack 4042781691, win 502, options [nop,nop,TS val 3966452277 ecr 668285845], length 0

Each line shows the sender (tcpdump writes the port after the address's last dot), the receiver and the flags: S for SYN, a dot for ACK. Notice the +1. A SYN carries no data, yet it uses up one sequence number, so its ACK is the ISN plus one. A FIN, the "I'm done" flag of the third section, uses up one number too.

The options are agreed once, here. mss 1460 is the biggest chunk of data either side accepts in one segment. That's 1,500 bytes, the largest packet this network carries (Routing, ICMP and traceroute met that limit), minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers, the labels at the front of every packet. The others, such as wscale and sackOK, help TCP go fast, and the next lesson, TCP performance, opens them up.

The phone picture breaks in one place. People on a call don't number their words, and a word never turns up a minute late. Packets can.

The handshake costs one round trip, the time for a message to go there and an answer to come back, before any data moves. On the lab network that's a tenth of a millisecond. To a bank's computer 70 ms away, it adds 70 ms to every new connection. That's the first reason to keep connections open and reuse them. Next, we'll see who answers the SYN, and what a client sees when nobody does.

aside.title: Does an ACK mean the bank's program got my payment?
aside.html: No. An ACK comes from the other machine's kernel, the moment the bytes land in its memory. The program there may not have read them yet, may crash before it does, or may fail to handle them. Only an answer from the program itself says the payment was dealt with. That's why the card reader waits for the bank's yes, and not for TCP's ACK.

sections.h: Who answers the call: listen, accept, and three ways a connect fails
sections.html:
The handshake in that capture happened inside the two kernels. The programs only asked for it. A program reaches the network through a socket: an object the kernel gives it that stands for one end of a conversation, and that it sends and receives through.

Think of an office with one phone number and many extensions. The IP address is the office's number, a port is an extension, and the kernel is the receptionist who answers every call.

A server program calls socket() to get a socket, bind() to claim port 9000, and listen() to say "I take calls on this extension". From then on, the kernel answers SYNs for port 9000 by itself. It finishes each handshake without asking the program, and puts the new connection in a queue, the accept queue, like a caller on hold. accept() takes one connection off that queue and hands the program a new socket for it. So a server has one listening socket per port, plus one connected socket per client.

How does the kernel tell all those connections apart? By four numbers: the client's address and port, and the server's address and port. That 4-tuple is the connection's name. Two connections may share any three of the numbers, never all four.

The number a program passes to listen(), the backlog, says how many callers may wait on hold. It's 50 for a Java ServerSocket unless you choose another, and Linux caps it with a setting called net.core.somaxconn (4096 by default since Linux 5.4). If a program stops calling accept() and the queue fills, the kernel starts ignoring new SYNs. Clients then see slow or failed connects, with no clear error.

A client program calls connect(). Its kernel picks a free local port for it, an ephemeral port (ephemeral means short-lived: the port belongs to this one connection). It sends the SYN, and the socket enters a state called SYN-SENT. connect() returns when the SYN-ACK has arrived and the kernel has sent the last ACK. That return is the first moment the client knows the server's machine is there.

A connect can fail in three ways, and each one sends you to look somewhere different. On the phone, a voice says nobody works at that extension, or the line stays silent, or a recording says the number isn't in use.

  • Connection refused. The SYN reached the machine, but no program listens on that port. Its kernel answers at once with an RST (reset), a segment that means "no such connection here". connect() fails within one round trip, and Java throws ConnectException: Connection refused. The machine is up and the network works. The program isn't running, or it's on another port.
  • Connect timed out. The SYN got no answer at all. A firewall (a program or device that blocks some traffic) may have dropped it. A router may have sent it nowhere, or the machine may be off, and the client can't tell which. So its kernel sends the SYN again. On this course's lab machines (Linux 6.12), it resends five times at 1-second gaps, then after 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 more seconds. It gives up about 136 seconds after the first SYN. Java's socket.connect(address, 5_000) stops waiting after 5 seconds instead: SocketTimeoutException: Connect timed out.
  • No route to host. The address belongs to your own local network, so before it sends anything, the kernel asks the network who has that address. That's ARP, the "who has this address?" question from the lesson The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP. Nobody answers. After three tries, about 3 seconds, the kernel gives up, and Java throws NoRouteToHostException.

A refusal is an answer, and a timeout is silence. Read them differently. Refused means the machine is alive and nothing listens on that port. A timeout means something in between drops packets without a word. And 136 seconds is far too long to keep a customer waiting at the till, so every client needs its own connect timeout.

The Try it below makes all three happen. Then we'll turn to the end of a connection's life.

In the RST, seq 0 and an ack of the SYN's seq + 1 are what RFC 9293 asks for when a SYN reaches a closed port, and the lab builds exactly that segment. The first run after the lab network starts can be a few milliseconds slower while ARP fills in its table.

sections.h: Closing a connection, one direction at a time
sections.html:
A TCP connection carries two streams of bytes, one each way, and each side ends its own. Back on the phone, one person says "That's all from me", and keeps listening while the other finishes. Then the other says "That's all from me too".

When your program calls close(), its kernel sends a FIN (finish), a segment that means "I have nothing more to send". The other kernel ACKs the FIN at once and tells its program: the next read() returns -1, which means end of stream. The other direction stays open. That side can go on sending until its program calls close() too, and its kernel sends a FIN of its own. So a clean close takes two FINs and two ACKs. Often an ACK rides along on a FIN or on data, as it did in the capture. (shutdownOutput() sends the same FIN but keeps the socket open for reading. That's what nc -N did, which is how the client could still read its echo.)

At every step, each socket is in a named state: the kernel's note of where the conversation has got to. ss -tan shows it. Follow the side that closes first, called the active closer:

  • FIN-WAIT-1: it sent its FIN and waits for the ACK.
  • FIN-WAIT-2: its FIN was ACKed, and it waits for the other side's FIN. It can still receive data: in the capture, the client got its 17-byte echo here.
  • TIME-WAIT: the other side's FIN arrived and was ACKed. The connection is over, but the kernel keeps a record of it for a while. The last section explains why.

The other side is the passive closer:

  • CLOSE-WAIT: the other side's FIN arrived. The kernel ACKed it, and now it waits for its own program to call close().
  • LAST-ACK: the program closed, its FIN went out, and the kernel waits for that FIN's ACK. Then the socket is gone.

Now add the states from the handshake: CLOSED (no connection), LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED (the server's half-open state) and ESTABLISHED (open and talking). Add the rare CLOSING, when both sides send a FIN at the same moment, and you have all eleven states in RFC 9293. The stepper below walks through the first Try it's connection, segment by segment.

CLOSE-WAIT is the state to remember, because it's always the program's doing. The other side has closed and the kernel has done its part. The socket waits for a close() that never comes, like a phone left off the hook. The causes are small. The program never read an answer to the end, or an error made it skip the code that closes. Or a pool, a set of open connections a program keeps for reuse, never threw out a dead one. Each stuck socket also holds a file descriptor (the number the program knows the socket by) until the program exits. A CLOSE-WAIT count that only grows is a leak in the program. Find the missing close().

There's also a rude way to end a connection: the RST from the last section, the phone slammed down. A kernel sends one when a segment arrives for a connection it doesn't have, like the SYN to port 9001. A program can ask for one too, by setting an option called SO_LINGER to 0 before it closes, which also throws away any data not yet sent. The other side's next read() or write() fails with "Connection reset by peer". An RST skips every closing state, TIME-WAIT included. That sounds handy, and the next section shows why it isn't the fix it seems.

frames.say: The client calls connect(). Its kernel picks port 50744 and a random starting number (the ISN), 244700535, sends the SYN and moves to SYN-SENT. The SYN carries no data, but it uses up one sequence number.

frames.say: The client writes 17 bytes. They're numbered 244700536 to 244700552, so the server's ACK says ack 244700553: the next byte it expects. Both sides stay ESTABLISHED for as long as they talk.

frames.say: The client is done sending (nc -N ends only its sending half, so it can still read). Its kernel sends a FIN at the next sequence number and moves to FIN-WAIT-1: it waits for the FIN to be ACKed. The FIN uses up one number, like the SYN.

frames.say: The server's kernel ACKs the FIN (ack 244700554, riding on the 17-byte echo) and moves to CLOSE-WAIT: the other side is done, but its own program isn't. The client, ACKed, moves to FIN-WAIT-2, and it still receives the echo. Each direction closes on its own.

frames.say: The server program calls close(). Its kernel sends its own FIN and moves to LAST-ACK. If this program never called close(), the socket would stay in CLOSE-WAIT for good.

frames.say: The client ACKs the server's FIN and moves to TIME-WAIT. When that ACK arrives, the server's side is CLOSED and forgotten. Ten segments in all, the same ten the Try it recorded.

try.title: Watch the states with ss
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. The lab box is one small Linux machine in Docker with network tools installed, and your labs folder appears inside it as /labs.

Read labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l07/demo/States.java. It opens one connection on 127.0.0.1 (the address a machine uses to talk to itself) and stops after each step to ask ss for the state of every socket on the server's port. The client closes first. The server program waits before it closes, like one that forgot.
Predict before you run it: after step 2, has the server program got the connection yet? After step 4, which side is in CLOSE-WAIT?

   (the same three sockets, LISTEN's Recv-Q back to 0)

4. client close(): its FIN was ACKed, but the server program has not closed
   State      Recv-Q Send-Q      Local Address:Port        Peer Address:Port
   LISTEN     0      50     [::ffff:127.0.0.1]:44169                  *:*
   CLOSE-WAIT 1      0      [::ffff:127.0.0.1]:44169 [::ffff:127.0.0.1]:48106
   FIN-WAIT-2 0      0      [::ffff:127.0.0.1]:48106 [::ffff:127.0.0.1]:44169

   server read() returned -1: end of stream, the peer has closed

In step 2, both ends are ESTAB (established) before accept() was called: the kernel finished the handshake alone. On a listening socket, the Send-Q column shows the backlog (50), and Recv-Q shows how many connections wait in the accept queue (1). After the client's close, the server sits in CLOSE-WAIT until its program closes. Its Recv-Q of 1 is the FIN, waiting to be read as end of stream. The side that closed first ends in TIME-WAIT. [::ffff:127.0.0.1] is an IPv4 address written in IPv6 form (IPv6 for application engineers explains it), because Java opens sockets that can speak both. On a Mac the demo runs without ss; watch netstat -an -p tcp there instead.

sections.h: TIME-WAIT: why a closed connection still holds a port
sections.html:
Now we can explain the opening's failure. The side that closes first keeps the connection in TIME-WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime (MSL), the longest a segment is assumed to survive somewhere in the network. RFC 9293 takes the MSL as 2 minutes, which makes 4. Linux waits a fixed 60 seconds instead. macOS waits 30, because it takes the MSL as 15 seconds. The wait does two jobs.

The last ACK may be lost. Then the other side, still in LAST-ACK, sends its FIN again. If the closer had already forgotten the connection, its kernel would answer that FIN with an RST. The other side would then report an error for a connection that closed cleanly. In TIME-WAIT, the closer recognizes the FIN and ACKs it again. On the phone, it's staying near the phone after "bye", in case the other person didn't hear you and asks again.

Old segments may still be on the way. A late copy of a segment from this connection could arrive after a new connection with the same 4-tuple has started, and land inside its sequence numbers. That's the stray segment from the first section. Keeping the 4-tuple out of use until any straggler must have died prevents it. The random ISNs make such a mix-up unlikely, and TIME-WAIT makes it safe.

A TIME-WAIT record is cheap in memory: no buffers (memory set aside for data), no program attached. What it holds is the 4-tuple. On a server that costs nothing, because the server's side is always the same address and port while the client's side varies. On a client it's a limit. Every connection from one machine to one server address and port needs its own local port. Linux hands out ephemeral ports from 32768 to 60999, which is 28,232 of them. Each one is held for 60 seconds after use. So a client that opens and closes connections to one destination can manage about 28,232 / 60 = 470 new connections a second. The next one fails at once with "Cannot assign requested address", a java.net.BindException in Java.

That's the opening's payments program. At 600 new connections a second to the bank, it used up all 28,232 ports in 47 seconds. The first ones still had 13 seconds of TIME-WAIT to go. Nothing was down. The program had run out of names for new connections. The Try it below does the same with only 10 ports.

The fix is to stop throwing connections away. A connection costs a round trip to open and a port for a minute after it closes. Keep it open and reuse it. That's what a connection pool does. Web programs call it HTTP keep-alive (HTTP is the language browsers and web servers speak): many requests, one after another, over one connection. Don't confuse it with TCP keepalive (the SO_KEEPALIVE option), which has nothing to do with reuse. It sends an empty test segment over a connection that has sat idle, by default for 2 hours on Linux, to check the other side is still there.

The settings people reach for first don't fix this. tcp_tw_reuse is a Linux setting that lets a new outgoing connection take a port still in TIME-WAIT, when the timestamps TCP adds to each segment make it safe. By default, it's on only for connections a machine makes to itself. Ending each connection with an RST (SO_LINGER set to 0) skips TIME-WAIT, but throws away data not yet sent and makes the other side report errors. Both treat the symptom. The cause is a new connection for every request.

There's one thing a connection can't tell us, though. It proves the other machine is there and that the numbers agree. It says nothing about how fast we may send, and that's where the next lesson picks up.

try.title: Run out of ports on purpose
steps: Start the privileged lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv. The everyday box isn't allowed to change kernel settings; this one is. The first line cuts its range of ephemeral ports to 10 and turns off tcp_tw_reuse, which would otherwise rescue connections the machine makes to itself. Both settings disappear when the box stops.
The next lines start an echo server and open 12 connections in a row, each one closed by the client first. Predict which connection fails first, and what the 13th attempt prints.
Then the box waits 70 seconds while TIME-WAIT runs out, and sends 12 messages over one connection instead.

Ten connections used the ten ports, and each port stayed in TIME-WAIT with a 60-second timer (-o shows it counting down). Connections 11 and 12 failed without sending a single packet: the kernel had no free port to put in the SYN. After the wait the count was 0, and one connection carried all 12 messages and left only 1 TIME-WAIT record behind. The timer can fire a few seconds late (the kernel's timer for such long waits is coarse), which is why the box waits 70 seconds and not 60. The same arithmetic at full size: 28,232 ports for 60 seconds is about 470 new connections a second to one destination.

opening:
Picture the busiest minute of lunch in a big city. Every tap of a card reaches one payments program, which asks the card's bank for a yes. For each payment, it opens a fresh connection, sends the question, reads the answer and closes the connection. Six hundred times a second.

Forty-seven seconds into the rush, payments start to fail with an odd message: Cannot assign requested address. The bank is fine, and so is the network.

It's easy to think a connection is free: open it, use it, close it, gone. That's how it looks from inside the program, where close() returns at once. The computer underneath remembers for longer.

In UDP and the sockets API, we sent single packets with no promise they'd arrive, and made them reliable by numbering and resending. TCP does that work for us, once both sides agree where the numbers start. In this lesson, we'll follow one connection from start to end, make one fail three ways, and run a computer out of ports on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payments program that failed at lunchtime with nothing broken. It opened a fresh connection for every payment, and each closed one kept a port for a minute after the program had forgotten it. Six hundred a second used up all 28,232 ports in under a minute.

On a Linux machine you can reach, ss -Htan state time-wait | wc -l counts the connections waiting out their minute, and ss -tan state close-wait looks for a missing close(). On a Mac, netstat -an -p tcp shows the same states.

Next, we'll make an open connection go fast, and find out why a fast link can still crawl when the other end is far away.

worked.title: Read the handshake byte by byte

steps.say: The SYN from the first Try it is 74 bytes long, and tcpdump can print them in hexadecimal (base 16, two digits per byte). The first 14 bytes are the local network's own header (Ethernet), and the next 20 are the IPv4 header, which starts 45. So TCP starts at byte 34, 0x22 in hexadecimal. Its first four bytes are the two ports.
Next come the sequence number, the acknowledgment number, the header's length and the flags. The ack is zero, because there's nothing to acknowledge yet.
steps.code:
0e95 d577   seq 244700535: the client's ISN
0000 0000   ack 0
a0          high 4 bits: 10 words = 40 bytes of TCP header, so 20 bytes of options
02          flags: SYN only
faf0        window 64240

steps.say: The options fill bytes 54 to 73. Walk them one at a time by their kind number: kind 1 is a one-byte NOP (padding), and every other kind is followed by its length. The lab's parser does the same walk to find the MSS.
steps.code:
0x0030:  faf0 1660 0000 0204 05b4 0402 080a ec6b
0x0040:  4235 0000 0000 0103 0307

02 04 05b4        MSS, length 4: 1460
04 02             SACK permitted, length 2
08 0a ...         timestamps, length 10
01                NOP: padding
03 03 07          window scale, length 3: shift by 7, multiply by 128

steps.say: The SYN-ACK's TCP header starts at the same place. Its seq is the server's ISN, and its ack is the client's ISN plus one, because the SYN used up one number. The seq is bigger than 2^31, so read those four bytes as a number that can't be negative (unsigned).

0x0020:  010a 2328 c638 f0f7 f3fa 0e95 d578 a012

12          flags: SYN + ACK

steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 14 fail for now. Segment.kt and TcpState.kt are finished. src/test/kotlin/sfz/net/l07/Captured.kt lists the ten segments of the first Try it's connection, copied from tcpdump's lines.
In TcpHeader.kt, write parse: the walk from the worked example, plus the loop over the options that finds the MSS. TcpHeaderTest feeds it the ten real frames.

TcpEndpoint.kt models one side of a connection, the state a kernel keeps for one socket. Write connect, send and close. Each returns one segment and moves sndNxt, the next sequence number this side will send, forward.

Write receive one state at a time, in the order its KDoc (the comment above the function) gives, and then tick, which ends TIME-WAIT once enough time has passed. TcpEndpointTest replays the recorded connection: your client and server endpoints must send the same segments the two kernels sent, and pass through the same states.
Then the last tests: a SYN to a closed port, a FIN repeated in TIME-WAIT, both sides closing at once, and a segment that arrives out of order. Run the tests until all 14 pass.
hints: ByteBuffer.wrap(frame).getInt(at).toLong() and 0xFFFF_FFFFL reads a 32-bit number that can't be negative. The SYN-ACK's seq, 4042781690, is bigger than Int.MAX_VALUE, so a plain getInt would give a negative number.
The options loop: when (kind) { 0 -> break; 1 -> at += 1; else -> { read the length byte; if kind is 2, read the MSS; at += length } }.
Every ACK you send is Segment(localPort, remotePort, sndNxt, rcvNxt, setOf(Flag.ACK), window). One private helper for it saves most of the typing.
In LISTEN, set sndNxt = isn + 1 when you return the SYN-ACK, so the ACK that completes the handshake arrives with ack == sndNxt.
Keep a private finSent flag. An ACK moves FIN-WAIT-1 to FIN-WAIT-2 only if it covers your FIN (seg.ack == sndNxt), and only after you sent one.

drill.title: Both sides' states, from memory
drill.prompt: No tools. A client connects to a server, sends one request, gets one answer and closes first, and the server closes right after. Write down the segments in order (who sends each one, and its flags), then the state of both sides after each segment arrives. Finish with three answers: which side holds TIME-WAIT, and for how long on Linux; which state would pile up if the server program never called close(); and what the client sees if nothing listens on the port.

answer.html:
segment                      client          server
                             CLOSED          LISTEN
1 client  -> SYN              SYN-SENT        SYN-RECEIVED
2 server  -> SYN-ACK          ESTABLISHED     SYN-RECEIVED
3 client  -> ACK              ESTABLISHED     ESTABLISHED   (accept() can return)
4 client  -> request [P.]     ESTABLISHED     ESTABLISHED
5 server  -> response [P.]    ESTABLISHED     ESTABLISHED   (ACKs ride along)
6 client  -> FIN              FIN-WAIT-1      CLOSE-WAIT    (server read() returns -1)
7 server  -> ACK              FIN-WAIT-2      CLOSE-WAIT
8 server  -> FIN              FIN-WAIT-2      LAST-ACK      (server program called close())
9 client  -> ACK              TIME-WAIT       CLOSED
  60 s later                  CLOSED

TIME-WAIT: the client, because it closed first; 60 s on Linux (30 s on macOS, 4 min in the RFC).
No close() on the server: CLOSE-WAIT piles up.
Nothing listening: an RST [R.] comes back at once, ConnectException: Connection refused.

recap: A connection opens with three segments, SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK, that swap two random starting numbers and cost one round trip. A SYN and a FIN each use up one sequence number, so their ACK is seq + 1.

The kernel does the handshake. listen() makes it answer SYNs for a port, accept() takes a finished connection off the queue, and each connection is named by its 4-tuple: both addresses and both ports.
Refused is an RST within one round trip: the machine is up and nothing listens. A timeout is silence: Linux resends the SYN for about 136 seconds unless the program sets its own connect timeout.

Each direction closes on its own. The side that closes first goes FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, TIME-WAIT; the other goes CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK. A CLOSE-WAIT count that only grows means a program never calls close().

TIME-WAIT (60 seconds on Linux) answers a lost last ACK and keeps stray old segments out of a new connection. It holds the 4-tuple, so a client opening new connections to one address runs out of ports near 470 a second. Reuse connections.
The limit: an open connection proves the other machine is there and that the numbers agree. It says nothing about how fast bytes may flow, which the next lesson takes up.

explain.prompt: A friend who looks after a payments program says: "Our machine has 20,000 connections in TIME-WAIT, so we're leaking connections. Let's set SO_LINGER to 0 so close() skips TIME-WAIT." Explain to them what TIME-WAIT is, which side has it and why, when it really hurts, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: TIME-WAIT isn't a leak. It's the record the side that closed first keeps after a clean close. Your program closes its connections, so the TIME-WAIT records are on your side, and Linux drops each one by itself after 60 seconds. It exists for two reasons. If your last ACK gets lost, the other side sends its FIN again, and you can still answer it instead of sending a reset. And stray old segments from the connection can't end up in a new connection with the same two addresses and ports. The records are cheap in memory, but each one holds a local port toward that destination. Linux has about 28,000 of them, so with one destination you hit a wall near 470 new connections a second, with "Cannot assign requested address". 20,000 records means you open about 330 connections a second, which tells me you aren't reusing them. SO_LINGER 0 would replace the clean close with a reset, throw away data not yet sent and make the other side report errors. I'd fix the cause: one long-lived client per destination, with a pool of connections that get reused and rarely closed.

deeper.html:
SYN floods and SYN cookies. A SYN that arrives at a listening socket creates a half-open entry in the kernel's SYN queue until the handshake's last ACK comes. An attacker who sends SYNs from fake addresses fills that queue, and real clients can't get in. Once the queue overflows, Linux answers with SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1): it stores nothing, encodes what it needs about the connection inside its own ISN, and rebuilds the connection from the ACK. That's one more reason the ISN isn't a plain counter.

Half-close from Java. socket.shutdownOutput() sends a FIN but keeps the socket readable, which is exactly what nc -N did in the first Try it. A protocol can use it to say "that's the whole request" without a length field; old HTTP/1.0 clients did. Most code never needs it, but it explains how a socket can be in FIN-WAIT-2 and still receive data.

Which timer is which. tcp_fin_timeout (60 s) is often mistaken for TIME-WAIT's length, and people raise or lower it to fight TIME-WAIT. It limits FIN-WAIT-2 for orphaned sockets, ones whose program has already closed. TIME-WAIT's 60 seconds is the constant TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN in the kernel's source code, and there's no setting for it. ss -tano shows both timers counting down.

Old fixes that made things worse. An old Linux setting, tcp_tw_recycle, shortened TIME-WAIT using timestamps. It broke clients behind NAT, whose timestamps come from many machines, and it was removed in Linux 4.12. SO_REUSEADDR is a different thing again: it lets a restarted server bind its port while old connections still linger, and it doesn't make TIME-WAIT go away. If a client truly needs more connections to one destination at once, add 4-tuples (more destination addresses, or more source addresses), not fewer seconds.

The SYN retry schedule. Kernels since mid-2023 resend a SYN at 1-second gaps first (net.ipv4.tcp_syn_linear_timeouts, 4 by default), then double the gap, up to tcp_syn_retries (6). The 136 seconds on the lab machines come from that schedule plus a last wait; older kernels show 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 seconds and about 127 s. Either way, the default is far too long for a customer waiting at a till.

TIME-WAIT on the server. A server that closes first (a web server that sends Connection: close, or one that closes idle connections) collects TIME-WAIT itself. That's the side that copes best: the 4-tuples vary by client, so they never collide. Some protocol designers let the server close first for exactly that reason.
